On a particular specialization of monomial symmetric functions

Vincent Brugidoua 00footnotetext: E-mail address vincent.brugidou@univ-lille.fr

a Université de Lille, 59655 Villeneuve d’Ascq cedex, France

Abstract : Let mλm_{\lambda} be the monomial symmetric functions with λ\lambda integer partition of n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{\ast}. For the specialization corresponding to the qq-deformation of the exponential, we prove that each mλm_{\lambda} is associated with a polynomial Jλ​(q)J_{\lambda}\left(q\right) whose coefficients belong to ℤ\mathbb{Z}. JλJ_{\lambda} is a generalization of the case λ=(n)\lambda=\left(n\right) for which J(n)=JnJ_{\left(n\right)}=J_{n} is the enumerator polynomial of inversions in trees on nn vertices. Some relations between JλJ_{\lambda} and Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} are obtained, these Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} having been introduced in [5]\left[5\right] from a qq-analog of certain symmetric functions, and being themselves inversion enumerator polynomials which generalize Jn(1)=JnJ_{n}^{\left(1\right)}=J_{n}. From the calculation of JλJ_{\lambda} for |λ|≤6\left|\lambda\right|\leq 6, we conjecture that the coefficients of each JλJ_{\lambda} are strictly positive and log-concave. As a consequence of Huh’s Theorem on the hh-vector of matroid complex ([8]\left[8\right]), it is shown that the coefficients of all Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} are strictly positive and log-concave, which gives a second argument in favor of these conjectures. It is also proven that the last n−1n-1 coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} are proportional to the first coefficients of column n−r−1n-r-1 of Pascal’s triangle, rr being the length of λ\lambda. This is a third argument to state the conjectures since the log-concavity of these columns are well known. The calculation of J(3,2,1)J_{\left(3,2,1\right)} shows the existence of an obstacle, if one wants to prove the conjectures by application of Huh’s theorem, cited above.

keywords : Monomial symmetric functions, q-deformation of the exponential, tree inversions, log-concavity, hh-vector of matroids.

1 Introduction

Let pn(r)p_{n}^{\left(r\right)} be the symmetric functions defined for any pair of integers (n,r)\left(n,r\right) such that n≥r≥1n\geq r\geq 1 by :

pn(r)=∑|λ|=n,l⁡(λ)=rmλp_{n}^{(r)}=\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n,\;l\left(\lambda\right)=r}m_{\lambda} (1.1)

where the mλ m_{\lambda\text{ }} are the monomial symmetric functions, the sum being over the integer partitions λ\lambda of nn, with length l⁡(λ)=rl(\lambda)=r. The functions pn(r)p_{n}^{(r)} are introduced with this notation in exercise 19 p.33 of [10]. In particular pn(1)p_{n}^{\left(1\right)} is the power symetric function pn=mnp_{n}=m_{n}. In [5] we have shown the following theorem for the specialization whose generating function of elementary symmetric function is given by Equation (1.2)\left(1.2\right) and sometimes called the q-deformation of the exponential.

Theorem 7.2 de [5]\left[5\right] : For n≥r≥1n\geq r\geq 1 and

Ex​p​(t)=∑n=0∞q(n2)​tnn!E_{xp}(t)=\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}q^{\binom{n}{2}}\dfrac{t^{n}}{n!} (1.2)

we have :

pn(r)=(1−q)n−r​q(r2)r!​(n−r)!​Jn(r)​(q)p_{n}^{(r)}=\left(1-q\right)^{n-r}\dfrac{q^{\binom{r}{2}}}{r!\left(n-r\right)!}J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}(q) (1.3)

where Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} is a monic polynomial with positive integer coefficients, a constant term equal to (n−r)!\left(n-r\right)! and which degree is (n−12)−(r−12)\binom{n-1}{2}-\binom{r-1}{2}. Moreover, for all r≥1r\geq 1 Jr(r)=1J_{r}^{\left(r\right)}=1.

[Note that the previously used Jn,rJ_{n,r} notation is now replaced by Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} to avoid confusion with the polynomials JλJ_{\lambda} introduced in this paper]

When r=1r=1 this gives :

mn=pn=pn(1)=(1−q)n−1(n−1)!​Jnm_{n}=p_{n}=p_{n}^{\left(1\right)}=\dfrac{\left(1-q\right)^{n-1}}{\left(n-1\right)!}J_{n} (1.4)

where Jn=Jn(1)J_{n}=J_{n}^{\left(1\right)} is the enumerator polynomial of inversions in trees on nn vertices introduced in [11]. More generally, we have seen that Jn(r)​(q)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}\left(q\right) are enumerator polynomials of inversions for sequences of ”colored” forests introduced by Stanley and Yan (see [17]\left[17\right]), or level statistics enumerators introduced by the author in Section 10 of [5]\left[5\right]. Alternatively the reciprocal polynomial of Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}, denoted Jn(r)¯\overline{J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}} in [5]\left[5\right], is the sum enumerator of generalized parking functions. We refer to [18] and [5]\left[5\right] for more details on these combinatorial interpretations.

When we take for λ\lambda the partition (n)\left(n\right), mλm_{\lambda} is factorized in the form of Equation (1.4)\left(1.4\right) for the specialization (1.2)\left(1.2\right). The question at the origin of our work is wether a similar factorization exists for all λ\lambda. We will see that the answer is positive and given by Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 3.5. The factorization of mλm_{\lambda} gives rise to a polynomial JλJ_{\lambda} whose coefficients belong to ℤ\mathbb{Z}, and which generalizes JnJ_{n}. This is proved by induction with two total orders on the set of integer partitions. It follows two recurrences allowing all JλJ_{\lambda} to be calculated with the initial condition J1=1J_{1}=1. From the calculations of JλJ_{\lambda} for n=|λ|≤6n=\left|\lambda\right|\leq 6, we conjecture that for any partition λ\lambda the coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} are positive and log-concave. A second argument for these conjectures is that it is possible to show the log-concavity of Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} using Huh’s results on the hh-vector of the matroid complex of representable matroids over a field of characteristic zero [8]\left[8\right]. We also prove that the last n−1n-1 coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} are proportional to the first n−1n-1 coefficients of column n−r−1n-r-1 of Pascal’s triangle. This gives a third argument for stating the conjectures since it is well known that these columns are log-concave. To conclude, it is underlined the need to strengthen the conjectures by continuing the calculations for larger values of |λ|\left|\lambda\right|. We also show by computing J(3,2,1)J_{\left(3,2,1\right)} that obtaining a complete proof of the log-concavity of JλJ_{\lambda} by an approach analogous to that used for Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} seems not possible.

where λ′=(λ1′,λ2′,..)\lambda^{\prime}=\left(\lambda_{1}^{\prime},\lambda_{2}^{\prime},..\right) is the conjugate of the partition λ\lambda. If rir_{i} is the number of parts of λ\lambda equal to i∈ℕ∗i\in\mathbb{N}^{\ast}, the sequence of multiplicity is m⁡(λ)=(r1,r2,…)m\left(\lambda\right)=\left(r_{1},r_{2},...\right), and we set |m⁡(λ)|=r1+r2+…=r\left|m\left(\lambda\right)\right|=r_{1}+r_{2}+...=r, m⁡(λ)!=r1!​r2!​…m\left(\lambda\right)!=r_{1}!r_{2}!...., we also write λ=1r1​2r2​…\lambda=1^{r_{1}}2^{r_{2}}....

In 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}, ⪯\preceq, ≤\leq and ⊑\sqsubseteq will respectively designate the reverse lexicographic order, the dominance order and the refinement order (see [10]\left[10\right] respectively p. 6, p.7 and p.103) It is known ([10]\left[10\right] Chap.1) that in 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} :

λ⊑μ⇒λ≤μ⇒λ⪯μ\lambda\sqsubseteq\mu\Rightarrow\lambda\leq\mu\Rightarrow\lambda\preceq\mu (2.2)

We generalize some definitions above to any strict composition of nn, i.e. any r-multiplet u=(u1,u2,…,ur)u=\left(u_{1},u_{2},...,u_{r}\right) of integers strictly greater than zero such that u1+u2+…+ur=nu_{1}+u_{2}+...+u_{r}=n, by setting |u|=u1+u2+…+ur\left|u\right|=u_{1}+u_{2}+...+u_{r}, l⁡(u)=rl(u)=r. 4 Conjectures about JλJ_{\lambda}

Three heuristic arguments lead us to state the following conjectures.

Conjecture 4.1

For any partition λ\lambda the coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} are strictly positive.

To state the second and third conjectures, let us recall some definitions. If a=(ak)0≤k≤na=\left(a_{k}\right)_{0\leq k\leq n} is a finite sequence of real numbers, then

  • *

    aa is unimodal if there is an index jj, 0≤j≤n0\leq j\leq n such that

    a0≤a1≤…≤aj−1≤aj≥aj+1≥…≥ana_{0}\leq a_{1}\leq...\leq a_{j-1}\leq a_{j}\geq a_{j+1}\geq...\geq a_{n}
  • *

    aa is log-concave (resp. strictly log-concave) if

    aj2≥aj−1aj+1 (resp. aj2>aj−1aj+1) for all 1≤j≤n−1 a_{j}^{2}\geq a_{j-1}a_{j+1}\text{ \ (resp. }a_{j}^{2}>a_{j-1}a_{j+1}\text{)\ \ for all \ }1\leq j\leq n-1\text{ \ }
  • *

    aa has no internal zeros if there do not exist i<j<ki<j<k satisfying

    ai≠0​aj=0​ak≠0a_{i}\neq 0\;\;\;a_{j}=0\;\;\;a_{k}\neq 0
  • *

    We will say that the polynomial Pa​(q)=a0+a1​q+…+an​qnP_{a}\left(q\right)=a_{0}+a_{1}q+...+a_{n}q^{n} has one of these properties if the sequence of its coefficients owns it.

More details on theses properties and a rich variety of unimodal and log-concave sequences can be found in the surveys [3]\left[3\right], [4]\left[4\right] and [15]\left[15\right].

Conjecture 4.2

For any partition λ\lambda, JλJ_{\lambda} is log-concave.

If these two conjectures are true then JλJ_{\lambda} is also unimodal (see Lemma 7.1.1 of [3]\left[3\right]), thus we can also state :

Conjecture 4.3

For any partition λ\lambda, JλJ_{\lambda} is unimodal.

Let us note that it is equivalent to formulate these conjectures for the polynomials JλJ_{\lambda}, MλM_{\lambda} or J^λ\widehat{J}_{\lambda}=Jλ/ΔJ_{\lambda}/\Delta, Δ\Delta being the GCD of the coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda}. The first argument for stating these conjectures results from the calculations already made. The conjectures are obviously true for J1nJ_{1^{n}} and J1n−2​2J_{1^{n-2}2} given by (3.21)\left(3.21\right) and (3.22)\left(3.22\right). And we have numerically checked them for |λ|≤6\left|\lambda\right|\leq 6. It is desirable to continue calculations for values of |λ|\left|\lambda\right| much bigger and that is what we are doing.

The second argument in favor of these conjectures comes from the fact that the coefficients of the polynomials Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} are strictly positive and log-concave. This is a consequence of Huh’s famous work and is in fact true for the larger class of polynomials denoted Im(a,b)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)} in [18]\left[18\right] ( Do not confuse the aa of Im(a,b)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)} with the sequence a=(ak)0≤k≤na=\left(a_{k}\right)_{0\leq k\leq n} above). We saw in [5]\left[5\right] that these polynomials are linked to Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} by Jn(r)=In−r(r​,1)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}=I_{n-r}^{\left(r,1\right)}. Polynomials Im(a,b)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)} and their reciprocal, which are the sum enumerators of the generalized classical parking functions, have been the subject of much research, a summary of which can be found in [18]. It is possible that the following properties are known to specialists but as we have not seen them in the literature (except the case In−1(1,1)=JnI_{n-1}^{\left(1,1\right)}=J_{n} ), we formulate them in the following proposition.

Proposition 4.4

The sequence of the coefficients of the polynomials Im(a,b)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)} (and their reciprocals) are strictly positive and log-concave, therefore unimodal.

Proof. Let

Im(a,b)​(q)=∑i=cdai​qiI_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)}\left(q\right)=\sum\limits_{i=c}^{d}a_{i}q^{i}

From the various properties of the polynomials Im(a,b)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)} and their reciprocals (see [18]\left[18\right] ) it is easy to see that c=0c=0, d=m​a+b​(m2)d=ma+b\binom{m}{2} and

a0=m!​ad=1a_{0}=m!\;\;\;a_{d}=1 (4.1)

In [17] p. 662, it is shown that

Im(a,b)​(1+t)=∑G′te⁡(G′)−mI_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)}\left(1+t\right)=\sum\limits_{G^{\prime}}t^{e\left(G^{\prime}\right)-m} (4.2)

where the sum is over the multicolor graphs G′G^{{}^{\prime}} without loop and whose vertex set is V={0,1,2,…,m}V=\left\{0,1,2,...,m\right\}. The edges of G′G^{\prime} between two vertices i,j≠0i,j\neq 0 are to be taken among the bb colored edges 0¯\overline{0}, 1¯\overline{1}, …, b−1¯\overline{b-1} and those between 00 and i≠0i\neq 0 are to be taken among the aa colored edges 0¯\overline{0}, 1¯\overline{1},…, a−1¯\overline{a-1}. e⁡(G′)e\left(G^{\prime}\right) is the number of edges of G′G^{\prime}. Let us now consider the graph introduced in [14] p. 3115 with the notation Km+1b,aK_{m+1}^{b,a}. This graph is defined as a complete graph on vertices V={0,1,2,…,m}V=\left\{0,1,2,...,m\right\} with the edges (i,j)\left(i,j\right), i,j≠0i,j\neq 0 of multiplicity bb and the edges (0,i)\left(0,i\right), i≠0i\neq 0 of multiplicity aa. It is clear that there is a bijection between the graphs G′G^{\prime} and the connected spanning graphs of Km+1b,aK_{m+1}^{b,a}. The Tutte polynomial of Km+1b,aK_{m+1}^{b,a} is :

T⁡(x,y)=∑A(x−1)c⁡(A)−1​(y−1)c⁡(A)+e⁡(A)−(m+1)T\left(x,y\right)=\sum\limits_{A}\left(x-1\right)^{c\left(A\right)-1}\left(y-1\right)^{c\left(A\right)+e\left(A\right)-(m+1)} (4.3)

where the sum is over the spanning graphs AA of Km+1b,aK_{m+1}^{b,a}, c⁡(A)c\left(A\right) being the number of connected components of AA, and e⁡(A)e\left(A\right) its number of edges. Comparison of (4.2)\left(4.2\right) and (4.3)\left(4.3\right) shows that

Im(a,b)​(q)=T⁡(1,q)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)}\left(q\right)=T\left(1,q\right) (4.4)

Let us consider now the matroid ℳ\mathcal{M} associated to Km+1b,aK_{m+1}^{b,a}. This matroid is graphical and therefore representable over any field ( Proposition 5.1.2 of [13]\left[13\right]), so its dual ℳ∗\mathcal{M}^{\ast}also ( Corollary 2.2.9 of [13]\left[13\right]). By noting T∗T^{\ast} the Tutte polynomial of ℳ∗\mathcal{M}^{\ast}, we have T∗​(y,x)=T⁡(x,y)T^{\ast}\left(y,x\right)=T(x,y), therefore Im(a,b)​(q)=T∗​(q​,1)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)}\left(q\right)=T^{\ast}\left(q,1\right). Let ρ\rho be the rank of ℳ∗\ \mathcal{M}^{\ast} and (h0,h1,…,h​ρ)\left(h_{0},h_{1},...,h\rho\right) be the hh-vector of the matroid complex I​N​(ℳ∗)IN\left(\mathcal{M}^{\ast}\right). It is known that ( see [1]\left[1\right] p.142) :

∑k=0ρhk​qρ−k=T∗​(q​,1)\sum\limits_{k=0}^{\rho}h_{k}q^{\rho-k}=T^{\ast}\left(q,1\right)

From Theorem 3 of [8]\left[8\right] it follows that Im(a,b)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)} is log-concave. Moreover, by the same theorem, we know that its coefficients have non internal zeros. But these coefficients are positive or zero (this comes for example, from their combinatorial definition). The internal coefficients are therefore strictly positive, so with (4.1)\left(4.1\right) all the coefficients are strictly positive. Unimodality follows from Lemma 7.1.17.1.1 of [3].  

The coefficients of polynomials Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}are therefore strictly positive and log-concave. In particular, the sequence of polynomials J(n)=Jn=Jn(1)J_{\left(n\right)}=J_{n}=J_{n}^{\left(1\right)}, satisfies both conjectures. We therefore have three sequences extracted from JλJ_{\lambda} which verify the conjectures ( i.e. λ=(n)\lambda=\left(n\right), 1n1^{n}, 1n−2​211^{n-2}2^{1}). Furthermore Equations (3.19)\left(3.19\right) and (3.20)\left(3.20\right) between JλJ_{\lambda} and Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} have strictly positive coefficients. All these facts provide the second argument in favour of the conjectures.

We will now see the third argument.

Pascalian coefficients, of MλM_{\lambda} (likewise for the parts and coefficients corresponding to JλJ_{\lambda} and J^λ\widehat{J}_{\lambda}).

c) Let us now make an induction on r=l⁡(λ)r=l\left(\lambda\right) with |λ|=n+1\left|\lambda\right|=n+1. The case r=1r=1 is proved by b). +(2​n−r−1−(n−1)n−1−(n−1))​qv⁡(λ(i))+n\displaystyle+\binom{2n-r-1-\left(n-1\right)}{n-1-\left(n-1\right)}q^{v\left(\lambda^{\left(i\right)}\right)+n}

r!n!​∑j′=0n−1(2​(n+1)−(r+1)−3−j′(n+1)−2−j′)​qv⁡(λ)+j′\dfrac{r!}{n!}\sum\limits_{j^{\prime}=0}^{n-1}\binom{2\left(n+1\right)-\left(r+1\right)-3-j^{\prime}}{\left(n+1\right)-2-j^{\prime}}q^{v\left(\lambda\right)+j^{\prime}}

which is indeed the Pascalian part Pn+1(r+1)P_{n+1}^{\left(r+1\right)} given by (5.2)\left(5.2\right).  

Here is now the proof of the conjectures of the section 4 for a part of the coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda}, which constitutes the third announced argument.

Corollary 5.2

For any partition λ\lambda such that λ≠1|λ|\lambda\neq 1^{\left|\lambda\right|}, the |λ|−1\left|\lambda\right|-1 last coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} are strictly positive and log-concave, then unimodal. If l⁡(λ)<|λ|−1l\left(\lambda\right)<\left|\lambda\right|-1 these coefficient are in fact strictly log-concave.

Proof.

It is known that the coefficients of the columns of Pascal’s triangle are strictly positif and log-concave. More precisely for any pair of integers (N,p)\left(N,p\right) such that p≥0p\geq 0 et N≥p+1N\geq p+1

(Np)2−(N+1p)​(N−1p)=(N!p!​(N−p)!)2​p\binom{N}{p}^{2}-\binom{N+1}{p}\binom{N-1}{p}=\left(\dfrac{N!}{p!\left(N-p\right)!}\right)^{2}p

So the columns of Pascal’s triangle are strictly log-concaves for p≥1p\geq 1, the column p=0p=0 consisting of 1 is only log-concave. The corollary follows for JλJ_{\lambda} and λ≠1|λ|\lambda\neq 1^{\left|\lambda\right|} from the proportionality, given by Theorem 5.1and Eq (3.17)\left(3.17\right), between Pascalian coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} and those of the column n−r−1n-r-1 of Pascal’s triangle.  

Incidentally it is easy to obtain a result similar to Theorem 5.1 for the polynomials Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} :

Corollary 5.3

For n−1≥r≥1n-1\geq r\geq 1 and 0≤i≤n−20\leq i\leq n-2

⟨q(n−12)−(r−12)−i⟩​Jn(r)=(n−r−1+in−r−1)\left\langle q^{\binom{n-1}{2}-\binom{r-1}{2}-i}\right\rangle J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}=\binom{n-r-1+i}{n-r-1} (5.9)

which means that the (n−1)\left(n-1\right) coefficients of Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} of the highest degree are given by the first coefficients of the column (n−r−1)(n-r-1) of Pascal’s triangle.

Proof.

Equations (3.13)\left(3.13\right) and (5.2)\left(5.2\right) successively give for n−1≥r≥1n-1\geq r\geq 1, m=d⁡(λ)−im=d\left(\lambda\right)-i and 0≤i≤n−20\leq i\leq n-2

⟨qm⟩​q(r2)​Jn(r)r!​(n−r)!=∑|λ|=n,l⁡(λ)=r⟨qm⟩​Mλm⁡(λ)!=(r−1)!(n−1)!​(n−r−1+in−r−1)​∑|λ|=n,l⁡(λ)=r1m⁡(λ)!\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle q^{\binom{r}{2}}\dfrac{J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}}{r!\left(n-r\right)!}=\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n,\;l\left(\lambda\right)=r}\dfrac{\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle M_{\lambda}}{m\left(\lambda\right)!}=\dfrac{\left(r-1\right)!}{\left(n-1\right)!}\binom{n-r-1+i}{n-r-1}\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n,\;l\left(\lambda\right)=r}\dfrac{1}{m\left(\lambda\right)!}

With (5.5)\left(5.5\right) and after simplification we obtain :

⟨qm⟩​q(r2)​Jn(r)=⟨qm−(r2)⟩​Jn(r)=(n−r−1+in−r−1)\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle q^{\binom{r}{2}}J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}=\left\langle q^{m-\binom{r}{2}}\right\rangle J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}=\binom{n-r-1+i}{n-r-1}

But by (3.3)\left(3.3\right)

m−(r2)=(n−12)+r−1−i−(r2)=(n−12)−(r−12)−im-\binom{r}{2}=\binom{n-1}{2}+r-1-i-\binom{r}{2}=\binom{n-1}{2}-\binom{r-1}{2}-i

which gives Equation (5.9)\left(5.9\right). Moreover Theorem 7.2 of [5]\left[5\right] shows that (n−12)−(r−12)\binom{n-1}{2}-\binom{r-1}{2} is the degree of Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}, which ends the proof.  

6 Further Developments

The first thing to do is to continue the calculations using recurrence (3.10)\left(3.10\right) and (3.15)\left(3.15\right) -or (3.18)\left(3.18\right) and (3.20)\left(3.20\right) if one prefers to work with integers- to numerically check the conjectures up to a value of n=n= |λ|\left|\lambda\right| as large as possible.

If these calculations do not contradict the conjectures, two ways can be considered to prove them.

The first way is to generalize the proof by induction of Theorem 5.1. The ideal would be to find a formula, generalizing that given by Theorem 5.1, to all coefficients. It would already be interesting to find a recurrence with coefficients in ℕ⁡[q]\mathbb{N}\left[q\right] (Recurrence (3.18)\left(3.18\right) has coefficients in ℤ⁡[q]\mathbb{Z}\left[q\right]…) to prove Conjecture 4.1.

The second way, of a combinatorial nature, would be to generalize to all the JλJ_{\lambda} (or J^λ\widehat{J}_{\lambda}) the method which made it possible to deduce the log-concavity of Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}. It would therefore be a question of associating with each J^λ\widehat{J}_{\lambda} a combinatorial object, itself associated with a matroid ℳλ\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} whose Tutte polynomial TλT_{\lambda} verifies the following analogue of (4.4)\left(4.4\right) :

J^λ​(q)=Tλ​(1,q)\widehat{J}_{\lambda}\left(q\right)=T_{\lambda}\left(1,q\right)

This way is more attractive than the first since it would allow to prove all the conjectures at the same time. Let us note in this regard that the log-concavity of the hh-vector of the matroid complex has recently been demonstrated for any matroid in [2]\left[2\right]. This allows the potentiel matroid ℳλ\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}, not to be limited to graphic matroids. However there is an obstacle to this way of doing thing. Indeed we calculated that :

J(3,2,1)​(q)=10+30​q+35​q2+35​q3+30​q4+20​q5+12​q6+6​q7+2​q8J_{\left(3,2,1\right)}\left(q\right)=10+30q+35q^{2}+35q^{3}+30q^{4}+20q^{5}+12q^{6}+6q^{7}+2q^{8}

22 and 3535 being coprime, J(3,2,1)J_{\left(3,2,1\right)} cannot be reduced to a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. But if we find a matroid ℳ\mathcal{M} of which the Tutte polynomial TT verifies J(3,2,1)​(q)=T⁡(1,q)J_{\left(3,2,1\right)}\left(q\right)=T\left(1,q\right). We would have with (1.23)\left(1.23\right) p.138 of [1]\left[1\right] :

T⁡(1,q)=∑(q−1)|A|−ρT\left(1,q\right)=\sum\left(q-1\right)^{\left|A\right|-\rho}

where the sum is over all the subsets AA of the ground set EE of ℳ\mathcal{M}, which ranks are equal to ρ\rho. The highest degree monomial of T⁡(1,q)T\left(1,q\right) is therefore clearly q|E|−ρq^{\left|E\right|-\rho}, so T⁡(1,q)T\left(1,q\right) would be monic which leads to a contradiction.

There are then, a priori, two possibilities :

* The obstacle mentioned above can be circumvented by remaining within the framework of matroids and theorems on the log-concavity attached to them.

* The obstacle is inherent to matroids and it will become necessary to associate combinatorially with JλJ_{\lambda} an algebraic or geometric structure distinct from matroids. One thinks for example of (graded ) posets (see chap. 3 of [16]\left[16\right]) or convex polytopes, interval greedoids, etc., for which log-concavity results have been proven or conjectured (see the already cited surveys [3]\left[3\right], [4]\left[4\right], [15]\left[15\right] and among others [6]\left[6\right], [9]\left[9\right]).
